{"problem_sha256":"76727f426e2aea072a2400056ac185544234543e1fc914fd12d3510aa2076e36","input_sha256":"db71e68fcd0a7e93b2e9114108edbe9b5cd731fbfec0f7e3aa850f9baa88eb95","read_receipts":[{"media_type":"text/markdown","object_id":"obj_01b4bef6b51e99b8a835b894a3e28388cebb5f26024329c431d7718d626af8de","sha256":"a0bef42e719f79b1d7a68ff8a1fd7015499ec750a4d3feb090f7847fc3984fa5","size_bytes":7282},{"media_type":"application/json","object_id":"obj_10e080778beba0ae7a6b7e3e3264384cf9f8c525768de288c3cf8cefb6ab6513","sha256":"68bedcb04f9964555042e31af6fdb707897448778d28dd468dc086b4e246388f","size_bytes":5086}],"usage":{"provider_requests":null,"total_tokens":null},"output":{"lemma_proposals":[{"statement":"For every nonzero rational x such that 1+x and 1-x are rational squares, there exist coprime integers m,n with n>0 and m not equal to 0 or to plus or minus n such that x=4mn(n^2-m^2)/(m^2+n^2)^2. Conversely, every such primitive pair defines a nonzero rational common neighbor of -1 and 1. If q=m^2+n^2 and r=q/gcd(q,2), then the reduced denominator of x is r^2; r is odd, r>=5, and each prime dividing r is congruent to 1 modulo 4. The reduced numerator of x is divisible by 24. These are individual-neighbor restrictions and imply no mutual-edge condition among several neighbors.","assumptions":["A common neighbor of -1 and 1 is a nonzero rational x for which 1+x and 1-x are rational squares.","The parameters m,n are integers with gcd(m,n)=1 and n>0."],"quantifiers":["For every nonzero rational common neighbor x, there is a primitive pair m,n with n>0, m nonzero, and m not equal to plus or minus n giving the displayed formula.","For every primitive pair m,n with n>0, m nonzero, and m not equal to plus or minus n, the displayed value has the stated reduced denominator and numerator properties."],"proof":"Choose rational u,v with u^2=1+x and v^2=1-x. Then u^2+v^2=2. Since x is nonzero, u is not 1. The line through (1,1) and (u,v) therefore has finite rational slope t=(v-1)/(u-1). Its second intersection with U^2+V^2=2 has coordinates U=(t^2-2t-1)/(t^2+1) and V=(1-2t-t^2)/(t^2+1). It follows that x=U^2-1=4t(1-t^2)/(1+t^2)^2. Write t=m/n in lowest terms with n>0. The condition x nonzero implies m is nonzero and m is not plus or minus n. Conversely, these parameter restrictions make x nonzero; the displayed circle parametrization gives rational square roots for 1+x and 1-x. Put q=m^2+n^2 and N=4mn(n^2-m^2), so x=N/q^2.

For any odd prime p dividing q, p divides neither m nor n. If p also divided n^2-m^2, then n^2 congruent to m^2 and to -m^2 modulo p, forcing p to divide 2m^2, a contradiction. Thus no odd prime dividing q divides N: such a prime divides neither mn nor n^2-m^2. If q is odd, m,n have opposite parity, so 8 divides N, and q^2 has no factor 2. If q is even, coprimality forces m,n odd; then q is congruent to 2 modulo 8 and 8 divides n^2-m^2. Hence the 2-adic valuation of N is at least 5 while that of q^2 is exactly 2, so precisely a factor of 4 cancels at 2. These facts give reduced denominator r^2, where r=q/gcd(q,2), and show r is odd.

If an odd prime p divides r, then m^2 is congruent to -n^2 modulo p and n is nonzero modulo p. Thus -1 is a quadratic residue modulo p, which implies p is congruent to 1 modulo 4. Also r>=5. If q is odd, q cannot be 1 or 3 as a sum of two nonzero squares, so q>=5 and r=q. If q is even, q is congruent to 2 modulo 8; r=1 would imply q=2 and m=plus or minus n, which is excluded, so r>=5.

The reduced numerator is divisible by 8: for odd q, mn is even; for even q, 8 divides n^2-m^2 and cancellation at 2 removes only a factor of 4. It is also divisible by 3. If 3 divides mn this is immediate; otherwise m and n are nonzero modulo 3, so their squares agree modulo 3 and 3 divides n^2-m^2. No factor of 3 is canceled in reducing x: if 3 divided q=m^2+n^2, the squares modulo 3 force both m and n to be divisible by 3, contrary to coprimality. Therefore the reduced numerator is divisible by both 8 and 3, hence by 24.","dependency_ids":[],"source_candidate_id":"cand_e2fdf6aa7d664d52a21c43ab0289c7a2"},{"statement":"For every finite set S of primes, there are infinitely many distinct sets {-1,1,x1,x2,x3,x4} of distinct nonzero rational numbers with 0<xi<1, such that every pairwise product-plus-one value involving an anchor is a rational square, and each xi*xj+1 for i<j is a square in Q_p for every p in S. This is only a finite-local statement: it does not assert that the six mutual values are rational squares.","assumptions":["S is any finite set of primes, possibly empty.","A square in Q_p means the square of an element of the p-adic field Q_p."],"quantifiers":["For every finite set S of primes.","There exist infinitely many distinct six-element sets satisfying the stated rational and p-adic square conditions."],"proof":"Let P be the product of the primes in S, taking P=1 when S is empty. For positive integers k, set L=1+kP and ti=iP/L for i=1,2,3,4. Define F(t)=4t(1-t^2)/(1+t^2)^2 and xi=F(ti). Since F'(0)=4, there is an interval (0,epsilon) on which F is strictly increasing and 0<F(t)<1. For all sufficiently large k, the ti lie in this interval and are strictly increasing in i. Thus the xi are distinct and in (0,1). As k increases, t1 strictly decreases, so x1 strictly decreases; since x1 is the least of the four xi, the resulting sets are infinitely many distinct sets.

Direct expansion gives 1+F(t)=((t^2-2t-1)/(1+t^2))^2 and 1-F(t)=((1-2t-t^2)/(1+t^2))^2. Thus each xi has rational-square edges to both anchors. The edge between -1 and 1 has value zero, also a rational square.

Fix p in S. Since p divides P and L is congruent to 1 modulo p, L is a p-adic unit and v_p(ti)>=1. The factors 1-ti^2 and 1+ti^2 are p-adic units. The formula for F shows v_p(xi)>=1 for odd p and v_2(xi)=2+v_2(ti)>=3 when p=2. Consequently, for y=xi*xj, v_p(y)>=1 for odd p and v_2(y)>=3 for p=2.

For odd p, 1+y has a square root in Z_p by the following lifting. Start with r1=1, a root of Z^2-(1+y) modulo p. If rh^2 is congruent to 1+y modulo p^h, write 1+y-rh^2=p^h d. Choose c modulo p so that 2rh c is congruent to d modulo p; this is possible because rh is a unit and p is odd. Then rh+cp^h is a root modulo p^(h+1). The resulting compatible approximations converge in Z_p to a square root.

For p=2, 1+y is congruent to 1 modulo 8. Start with the odd root r3=1 modulo 8. If odd rh satisfies rh^2 congruent to 1+y modulo 2^h for h>=3, replacing it by rh+2^(h-1) changes its square by 2^h rh+2^(2h-2), which is congruent to 2^h modulo 2^(h+1). Thus one of rh and rh+2^(h-1) is a root modulo 2^(h+1); choose it as r(h+1). The successive changes have valuations tending to infinity, so these approximations converge in Z_2, and their limit squares to 1+y. Applying the appropriate lifting to every pair i<j gives all six asserted local-square conditions for each p in S. This proof supplies local roots only at primes in the specified finite set and does not give rational roots for the mutual values.","dependency_ids":[],"source_candidate_id":"cand_3684c0a9b6a7469a907446dafb5d1d94"}]}}
